$comment: Single source of truth for every THL tool. Consumed by toolkit.js (browser runtime + argument docs), nlp.js (parser vocabulary), interface.js (assistant capabilities) and the thehallucinatedlab Python package. Adding a tool here is what makes it appear in all four. Each tool carries a "status": "live" tools are public, "dev" tools are visible only in dev mode and are never shown to a visitor. Keep python/thehallucinatedlab/data/manifest.json byte-identical: scripts/sync-spec.js copies it and test/manifest.test.js fails the build if they drift.

scoring.$comment: How the intent parser scores a tool against an utterance. Weights are additive, capped at 1.0, and a tool is only matched at or above the threshold. Tuned so an action word alone ('convert 100 usd to eur') stays below the bar while an action plus a real signal clears it.

tools.name: convert
tools.title: Convert
tools.summary: Convert an image between formats without uploading it anywhere.
tools.description: Re-encodes an image into another format. In the browser this runs on a canvas, so the file never leaves the page; in Python it runs through Pillow. Formats without an alpha channel are flattened onto a background colour first, so a transparent PNG becomes a JPEG with a solid backdrop rather than a black one.

input.maxPixelsNote: Roughly 40 megapixels. The browser encodes on the main thread, so a larger input would lock the tab.

params.name: format
params.description: The format to convert to.
params.prompt: Which format do you want — png, jpeg, webp or avif?

params.name: quality
params.description: Encoder quality, 1-100. Higher keeps more detail and produces a larger file. Ignored for PNG, which is lossless.

params.name: background
params.description: Colour used to flatten transparency when the target format has no alpha channel. Only JPEG needs this.

examples.text: make it a jpg at 80 quality

tools.name: extract
tools.title: Extract
tools.summary: Turn a document into Markdown with its structure intact.
tools.description: Reads a PDF, Word file, presentation, spreadsheet, web page or e-book and writes Markdown. Headings stay headings and page boundaries stay marked, because that is exactly what the next stage splits on -- flattening to plain text first would leave structure-aware chunking with no structure to be aware of. In the browser this runs on vendored parsers in your own tab; in Python it runs through LangChain's document loaders, which reach considerably more formats.

input.maxBytesNote: 100MB. The browser holds the whole file in memory while parsing, so a larger document would exhaust the tab.

params.name: format
params.description: What to write. Markdown keeps headings and tables; text flattens everything. Choosing text means the chunk tool has no structure left to split on, so pick it only when the document is going somewhere else.

params.name: frontmatter
params.description: Write a YAML block at the top recording the source filename, page count and extraction time. Turn it off when the output is going somewhere that would render the block as body text.

params.name: page_markers
params.description: Mark page boundaries with an HTML comment. Markdown renderers ignore them and the chunk tool reads them, which is what lets a retrieved chunk cite the page it came from.

params.name: tables
params.description: Render tables as Markdown tables rather than flattening them to lines of text. Off is occasionally better for documents where the parser mistakes a layout grid for a data table.

meta.$comment: Which formats each runtime can actually read today. browser is what the page parses with no parser at all -- DOMParser, FileReader and a CSV reader -- so it stays true with nothing vendored and nothing installed. python is what the extract extra installs. The page compares the two to decide when to offer the bridge. Vendoring pdf.js and mammoth into assets/vendor would move .pdf and .docx into the browser tier; until something is actually vendored, listing them here would make the page offer a parser it does not have.

structure.$comment: Where headings come from in each format. Anything absent here yields page or section markers only, never invented headings.

examples.text: read the document as plain text

tools.name: chunk
tools.title: Chunk
tools.summary: Split a Markdown document into retrieval-sized pieces along its own structure.
tools.description: Splits on headings first and size second, so a chunk is a section of the document rather than an arbitrary window of characters. Each piece carries the heading path it came from and the page it started on, which is what lets a retrieved chunk cite its source instead of arriving as anonymous text. Output is JSONL -- one record per line, text plus metadata, the same shape a LangChain Document has.

input.maxBytesNote: 100MB. Chunking holds the document and its pieces in memory at once.

params.name: max_tokens
params.description: The largest a chunk may be. 512 suits most retrieval; larger chunks carry more context but blur what a match actually matched. The ceiling is BGE-M3's context window.

params.name: overlap
params.description: Tokens repeated from the end of one chunk at the start of the next, so a sentence split across a boundary is still whole somewhere. Must be smaller than max_tokens.

params.name: tokenizer
params.description: What counts a token. bge matches the model the embed stage uses, and is the only one whose counts are exact for this pipeline. estimate needs no download and deliberately over-counts.

params.name: heading_context
params.description: Prepend the heading path to each chunk's text. Costs a few tokens per chunk and makes a fragment from deep in a document embed as what it is rather than as a stray paragraph.

meta.$comment: Real tokenizer identities. The enum values are single alphabetic words because the intent parser tokenizes on [a-z]+ and would split 'bge-m3' into 'bge', 'm', '3', so a hyphenated value could never be matched from an utterance.

bge.note: Downloads roughly 17MB -- the tokenizer alone, not the 2.3GB model.

openai.note: For estimating against OpenAI models. Wrong for this pipeline: BGE-M3 uses a different vocabulary entirely.

estimate.note: No download and no dependency. Over-counts on purpose, so a chunk sized by it never overflows the real tokenizer.

tools.name: tokenize
tools.title: Tokenize
tools.summary: Count tokens, so you know what a corpus costs before you embed it.
tools.description: Reports how many tokens a document or a folder of chunks contains, how they are distributed, and how many pieces exceed the model's context window. This is a measuring instrument, not a stage of the pipeline: an embedding model tokenizes internally with its own vocabulary, so there is no such thing as handing it a pre-tokenized file. What the tokenizer is genuinely for is deciding how to chunk and knowing what embedding will cost.

params.name: tokenizer
params.description: What counts a token. bge matches the embed stage exactly; openai is for costing against a different model; estimate needs no download.

params.name: limit
params.description: The context window to measure against. Anything longer is reported as an overflow, because at embed time it would be silently truncated and the tail would simply not be in the vector.

tools.name: embed
tools.title: Embed
tools.summary: Turn chunks into vectors with a model that runs on your own machine.
tools.description: Reads the JSONL that chunk produced and writes one vector per record. BGE-M3 is the default: 1024 dimensions, 8192 context, and multilingual without a separate model per language. Vectors are L2-normalised by default, which makes cosine similarity and dot product the same operation and is what most vector stores assume. Output is a single .npy alongside the ids, not one file per chunk -- a corpus of 40,000 chunks is 40,000 files nobody wants.

params.name: model
params.description: Which embedding model. bge is BAAI/bge-m3 at 1024 dimensions -- multilingual, 8192 context, roughly 2.3GB. minilm is all-MiniLM-L6-v2 at 384 dimensions: far smaller and faster, English-centric, 512 context. They are not interchangeable after the fact, because an index built with one cannot be queried with the other.

params.name: batch_size
params.description: How many chunks to encode at once. Larger is faster until it exhausts memory; on CPU the useful range is small.

params.name: normalize
params.description: Scale every vector to unit length, so cosine similarity and dot product agree. Leave it on unless the store you are feeding expects raw magnitudes.

meta.$comment: Dimensions are not a detail. An index built at 1024 and queried at 384 either errors or, worse, silently returns nonsense -- which is why index records the model that produced it.

bge.note: Multilingual. No instruction prefix needed, unlike bge-large-en.

minilm.note: English-centric. Chunks longer than 512 tokens are truncated.

tools.name: index
tools.title: Index
tools.summary: Build a portable vector database you own and can query with your own code.
tools.description: Takes the vectors and the chunks they came from and writes a database directory. Crucially it also writes a sidecar recording which model produced the vectors, how many dimensions they have, and whether they were normalised -- without that, the folder is not actually usable: opening a Chroma collection and calling query_texts reaches for its own default embedder at 384 dimensions, which against 1024-dimension vectors either raises or silently returns nonsense. A query snippet is written alongside, so the first thing you can do with the output is use it.
tools.$pageComment: vector-index.html, not index.html: the tool is named 'index' but index.html is the site homepage, and the manifest test asserts this file exists -- pointing at it would have invited overwriting 27KB of homepage.

params.name: store
params.description: chroma writes a sqlite-backed collection with nearest-neighbour search built in. numpy writes a .npy plus a JSONL of metadata and no database at all -- portable anywhere, readable in four lines, and the right choice when you intend to load it into something else.

params.name: collection
params.description: What to call the collection inside the store. Chroma requires 3-63 characters, starting alphanumeric.

params.name: overwrite
params.description: Replace an existing collection of the same name. Off by default, because appending vectors from a different model to an existing index is the failure that is hardest to notice afterwards.

meta.$comment: FAISS is deliberately absent. LangChain's FAISS wrapper pickles its docstore and now requires allow_dangerous_deserialization=True to load, which is the wrong default for a tool whose entire purpose is handing someone a database to open later.

tools.name: describe_dataset
tools.title: Describe dataset
tools.summary: Read a data file and report its shape, plus an inferred type and a confidence for every column.
tools.description: The cheap first pass over a tabular file. Reports rows, columns, null counts, cardinality and a preview for each column, alongside an inferred type and a confidence score in [0,1]. Anything below 0.7 is flagged rather than asserted, because the failures people actually notice are misclassifications: a zip code read as a quantity, a 0/1/2 encoding given a mean, dates in three formats silently coerced. Nothing is written and nothing is charted.

params.name: sample
params.description: Rows to sample. Omitted, the file is read whole unless it is large enough to need streaming.

params.name: delimiter
params.description: Field separator. Sniffed when omitted; what you pass is obeyed rather than treated as a hint.

params.name: encoding
params.description: Text encoding. Sniffed when omitted.

params.name: header
params.description: Header row index. Pass -1 for a file with no header row.

params.name: na_values
params.description: Extra tokens to read as null, on top of the ones pandas already knows.

params.name: sheet
params.description: Worksheet name for a spreadsheet, or 'all' to treat each sheet as its own dataset.

params.name: nrows
params.description: Read only the first N rows.

params.name: types
params.description: Column-to-type overrides applied after inference, for example zip=categorical_high.

params.name: seed
params.description: Sampling seed, recorded in the recipe so a rerun draws the same rows.

tools.name: profile_column
tools.title: Profile column
tools.summary: Compute the summary statistics that fit one column's inferred type.
tools.description: Runs the statistics the registry marks default for the column's type, or an explicit list. A statistic that raises is recorded on the result rather than losing the other forty. Outlier counts always ship with the rule that produced them, because a count with no rule attached is not a statistic: the IQR fence and three sigma disagree by a factor of several on the same column.

params.name: column
params.description: Which column to profile.

params.name: summaries
params.description: Which statistics to run. Defaults to the ones marked default for the column's type.

params.name: type_override
params.description: Read the column as this type instead of the inferred one.

params.name: top_n
params.description: Cut-off for level and token listings.

params.name: outlier_rule
params.description: How outliers are counted. The rule is reported alongside the number.

tools.name: plot_column
tools.title: Plot column
tools.summary: Draw one figure for one column and write it to a file.
tools.description: Charts are matplotlib on the Agg backend, selected per column type. A horizontal bar is the default for a low-cardinality category rather than a pie, because people compare lengths well and angles badly; pie and donut stay available for the cases where share-of-whole is the actual point. Asking for a chart the column's type does not support is an error that names the types it does.

params.name: column
params.description: Which column to plot.

params.name: chart
params.description: Which chart. Each applies only to certain column types, and the error names which.
params.prompt: Which chart - histogram, box, hbar or line?

params.name: out
params.description: Where to write. Defaults to the figures directory beside the source file.

params.name: target
params.description: Required by stacked_vs_target, ignored by every other chart.

params.name: figure_format
params.description: Image format.

params.name: dpi
params.description: Resolution, for raster output.

params.name: top_n
params.description: Cut-off for charts of high-cardinality columns.

tools.name: relate_columns
tools.title: Relate columns
tools.summary: Measure how columns relate: correlation, missingness, duplicates, or a target.
tools.description: The tier that makes this exploratory data analysis rather than a describe() wrapper. Pearson and Spearman for numeric pairs and a bias-corrected Cramer's V for categorical ones; which columns go missing together, since two columns null on the same rows are usually one uncollected fact rather than two gaps; exact and near-duplicate row counts with 'near' defined in the output; and, where a target is named, a mutual-information ranking of every feature against it.

params.name: kind
params.description: Which analysis to run.
params.prompt: Which - correlation, missingness, duplicates or target?

params.name: columns
params.description: Restrict the analysis to these columns.

params.name: target
params.description: Required by kind=target; enables target-versus-feature views elsewhere.

params.name: out
params.description: Where figures go. Defaults to the figures directory beside the source file.

params.name: top_n
params.description: Cut-off for the rankings and the level breakdowns.

tools.name: eda_report
tools.title: EDA report
tools.summary: Render a complete profile report from a fully specified recipe.
tools.description: The seam the design turns on. A recipe holds every decision a run makes - column types, chart selections, the sampling seed, the output format - and this renders one. The interactive session's only job is to produce a recipe; a CI job checks one into a repository; a future browser front-end would build one too. All of them arrive here, so there is one code path rather than three, and a saved recipe replays identically on next month's export.

params.name: recipe
params.description: A recipe file. Produced by --save-recipe or by the interactive session.

params.name: out
params.description: Output directory. Defaults to a single new directory beside the source file.

params.name: format
params.description: Markdown diffs in a pull request; a self-contained HTML blob does not.

params.name: self_contained
params.description: Inline every figure as base64 so the report is one file. HTML only.

params.name: overwrite
params.description: Write into a directory this tool did not create.
